terms.definition: Placing pupils in a class for all subjects according to their ability.
terms.examiner: Distinguish it from setting (ability groups subject by subject). Ball and Gillborn and Youdell show the lower streams are disproportionately working class.

terms.definition: Grouping pupils by ability separately in each subject.
terms.examiner: Do not treat setting and streaming as the same thing; mark schemes credit the distinction.

terms.definition: Sorting pupils into those who will pass anyway, those who can be helped to pass, and hopeless cases, then focusing on the middle group.
terms.examiner: Gillborn and Youdell. Link it to league tables and the A-to-C economy.

terms.definition: The teacher's picture of the perfect pupil, usually one with middle-class, white, often female characteristics.
terms.examiner: Becker's idea, extended by Archer. Use it to explain labelling of working-class and minority ethnic pupils.

terms.definition: A group of pupils who share similar values and behaviour patterns.
terms.examiner: Lacey: they form as a result of streaming. Name the type (pro- or anti-school) when you apply it.

terms.definition: The process of teachers categorising pupils according to how they see their ability or attitude.
terms.examiner: Lacey's term, paired with polarisation. Explain the link between the two for a developed point.

terms.definition: Pupils responding to streaming by moving to one of two opposite poles, pro-school or anti-school.
terms.examiner: Lacey's term. Show how it leads to subcultures rather than just defining it.

terms.definition: A group that gains status by rejecting the school's values, for example by truanting or messing around.
terms.examiner: Willis's lads are an example. Say how it lowers achievement and why pupils join it (status frustration).

terms.definition: Willis's term for the lads' culture of resistance, which prepared them for manual work.
terms.examiner: Use it to challenge correspondence theory: the lads chose their path.

terms.definition: The sense of self pupils form at school, shaped by class, gender and ethnicity and by how teachers see them.
terms.examiner: Archer's 'Nike identities' are a good example of working-class identity clashing with school.

terms.definition: The beliefs a teacher holds about how well a pupil will do, which may shape how the teacher treats them.
terms.examiner: Rosenthal and Jacobson's Oak School study is the classic evidence; later studies have struggled to repeat it, which gives you an evaluation point.

terms.definition: Woods's range of pupil responses: ingratiation, ritualism, retreatism and rebellion.
terms.examiner: Use them to evaluate Lacey's simple pro/anti split: real responses are more varied.
